title: MATH GAOKAO - 7
description: Authentic-style mathematics problems inspired by China’s Gaokao — build deeper understanding, sharper thinking, and real exam readiness.

questions.learningObjective: Find the intersection of two finite sets given in roster notation.
questions.question: Let \(A=\{1,2,3\}\) and \(B=\{2,3,4\}\). What is \(A\cap B\)?
questions.explanation: The intersection \(A\cap B\) contains exactly the elements that belong to both \(A\) and \(B\). Comparing \(A=\{1,2,3\}\) and \(B=\{2,3,4\}\), the common elements are \(2\) and \(3\). Therefore \(A\cap B=\{2,3\}\).
questions.hint: List the elements that appear in both sets.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the identity property of the empty set under intersection.
questions.question: For any set \(A\), what is \(A\cap\varnothing\)?
questions.explanation: The empty set \(\varnothing\) has no elements. Therefore no element can belong to both \(A\) and \(\varnothing\). Hence \(A\cap\varnothing=\varnothing\).
questions.hint: Recall that the empty set contains no elements.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the intersection of two overlapping real intervals.
questions.question: Let \(A=[1,4)\) and \(B=(2,5]\). What is \(A\cap B\)?
questions.explanation: The interval \(A=[1,4)\) contains all real numbers from \(1\) up to but not including \(4\). The interval \(B=(2,5]\) contains all real numbers greater than \(2\) up to and including \(5\). Their common part consists of real numbers greater than \(2\) and less than \(4\). Therefore \(A\cap B=(2,4)\).
questions.hint: Find the overlap of the two intervals and check which endpoints are included.

questions.concept: Intersection of Sets Given in Set-Builder Notation
questions.learningObjective: Convert two sets from set-builder notation to roster form and find their intersection.
questions.question: Let \(A=\{x\in\mathbb Z\mid -1\le x\le 3\}\) and \(B=\{x\in\mathbb N^+\mid x<4\}\). What is \(A\cap B\) in roster form?
questions.explanation: The set \(A\) consists of the integers from \(-1\) to \(3\), so \(A=\{-1,0,1,2,3\}\). The set \(B\) consists of positive integers less than \(4\), so \(B=\{1,2,3\}\). The common elements are \(1,2,3\). Therefore \(A\cap B=\{1,2,3\}\).
questions.hint: Write each set in roster form first, then identify the elements they share.

questions.learningObjective: Use the inclusion–exclusion principle to find the number of elements in an intersection.
questions.question: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be finite sets with \(|A|=10\), \(|B|=8\), and \(|A\cup B|=14\). How many elements are in \(A\cap B\)?
questions.explanation:
By the inclusion–exclusion principle,
\[
|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|.
\]
Substituting the given values gives
\[
14=10+8-|A\cap B|.
\]
Thus
\[
|A\cap B|=10+8-14=4.
\]
Therefore \(A\cap B\) has \(4\) elements.
questions.hint: Use the formula relating the sizes of two sets, their union, and their intersection.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the property of the universal set under intersection.
questions.question: Let \(U\) be the universal set and \(A\subseteq U\). What is \(A\cap U\)?
questions.explanation: Since \(A\subseteq U\), every element of \(A\) is already an element of \(U\). Therefore the elements common to \(A\) and \(U\) are exactly the elements of \(A\). Hence \(A\cap U=A\).
questions.hint: Consider which elements belong to both \(A\) and the universal set.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the intersection of two disjoint finite sets.
questions.question: Let \(A=\{1,2\}\) and \(B=\{3,4\}\). What is \(A\cap B\)?
questions.explanation: The sets \(A=\{1,2\}\) and \(B=\{3,4\}\) have no common elements. Therefore their intersection is the empty set, so \(A\cap B=\varnothing\).
questions.hint: Check whether any element appears in both sets.

questions.learningObjective: Determine an unknown element that makes an intersection equal to a given set.
questions.question: Let \(A=\{1,2,a\}\) and \(B=\{1,3\}\). If \(A\cap B=\{1,3\}\), what is the value of \(a\)?
questions.explanation: For \(A\cap B=\{1,3\}\), the element \(3\) must belong to both \(A\) and \(B\). Since \(3\in B\) already, we need \(3\in A\). The set \(A=\{1,2,a\}\) contains \(3\) only if \(a=3\). Checking, if \(a=3\), then \(A=\{1,2,3\}\) and \(A\cap B=\{1,3\}\), as required. Therefore \(a=3\).
questions.hint: Use the fact that every element of the given intersection must belong to both sets.

questions.concept: Intersection of Unbounded and Bounded Intervals
questions.learningObjective: Determine the simplified interval form of the intersection of two real intervals.
questions.question: Let \(A=(-\infty,3]\) and \(B=(0,5)\). What is \(A\cap B\)?
questions.explanation:
The interval \(A=(-\infty,3]\) contains all real numbers less than or equal to \(3\). The interval \(B=(0,5)\) contains all real numbers greater than \(0\) and less than \(5\). Their common part consists of real numbers greater than \(0\) and at most \(3\). Therefore
\[
A\cap B=(0,3].
\]
questions.hint: Find the overlapping region and check whether \(0\) and \(3\) belong to both intervals.

questions.concept: Intersection of Integer Sets Defined by Inequalities
questions.learningObjective: Convert two sets defined by inequalities over the integers into roster form and find their intersection.
questions.question: Let \(A=\{x\in\mathbb Z\mid x^2\le 9\}\) and \(B=\{x\in\mathbb Z\mid -2<x\le 4\}\). What is \(A\cap B\) in roster form?
questions.explanation:
The inequality \(x^2\le 9\) is equivalent to \(-3\le x\le 3\), so
\[
A=\{-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3\}.
\]
The inequality \(-2<x\le 4\) gives the integers
\[
B=\{-1,0,1,2,3,4\}.
\]
The common elements are \(-1,0,1,2,3\). Therefore
\[
A\cap B=\{-1,0,1,2,3\}.
\]
questions.hint: Write both sets in roster form first, then list the elements that appear in both.
